module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Under standard HTTP semantics, which method is both safe and idempotent for retrieving a resource representation?

options.A: PATCH
options.B: POST
options.C: GET
options.D: DELETE

explanation: GET requests retrieval without asking for a state-changing action and is idempotent. DELETE is idempotent but not safe; POST and PATCH have no general idempotency guarantee.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A POST successfully creates a new resource, and the server can identify its URI. Which response most directly communicates creation?

options.A: 201 Created, normally with a Location header identifying the resource
options.B: 200 OK as a mandatory creation-only status
options.C: 404 Not Found with the new resource representation
options.D: 301 Moved Permanently as a creation acknowledgment

explanation: 201 specifically indicates creation. Location can identify the primary new resource; 200 is a general success code rather than the creation-specific choice.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Which mapping of HTTP response status families is correct?

options.A: 4xx: successful responses; 5xx: redirections
options.B: 4xx: informational responses; 5xx: successful responses
options.C: 4xx: redirections; 5xx: informational responses
options.D: 4xx: client-error responses; 5xx: server-error responses

explanation: HTTP assigns client errors to the 4xx class and server errors to the 5xx class. The classes describe response semantics, not which party must always change code.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A normal GET succeeds and returns the requested representation without a redirect or conditional-cache result. Which status is appropriate?

options.A: 301 Moved Permanently
options.B: 201 Created
options.C: 200 OK
options.D: 500 Internal Server Error

explanation: 200 indicates successful processing; for GET, its content normally represents the target resource.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: An existing public page has moved permanently to a new URI, and the response supplies that URI in Location. Which listed status expresses that permanent redirect?

options.A: 304 Not Modified
options.B: 301 Moved Permanently
options.C: 503 Service Unavailable
options.D: 400 Bad Request

explanation: 301 communicates a permanent URI change. 304 is a conditional-request result, not a redirect to a new page.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: The origin server has no current representation for a requested URI and chooses to report that absence. Which status fits?

options.A: 201 Created
options.B: 404 Not Found
options.C: 200 OK
options.D: 502 Bad Gateway

explanation: 404 reports that no current representation was found or that the server is unwilling to disclose one. This scenario explicitly reports absence.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Which browser storage mechanism is automatically attached to eligible HTTP requests according to its scope, attributes, credentials mode, and browser policy?

options.A: sessionStorage entries
options.B: Cookies
options.C: All JavaScript variables in the page
options.D: localStorage entries

explanation: Browsers generate Cookie headers for eligible stored cookies. Web Storage and ordinary variables are not automatically serialized into HTTP requests.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A resource API supports complete replacement of a representation and partial modification of specified fields. Which method pairing best matches those intended operations?

options.A: POST is the only method capable of either operation
options.B: PUT for replacement; PATCH for partial modification
options.C: PATCH for complete replacement only; GET for partial modification
options.D: GET for replacement; DELETE for partial modification

explanation: PUT expresses creation or replacement of target state using the supplied representation. PATCH applies a patch document. The precise accepted representations and patch format are API-defined.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: The first DELETE /items/7 removes an existing item and returns success. A repeated identical DELETE returns 404 because the item is already absent. Is that status difference alone a violation of DELETE idempotency?

options.A: No; the intended final state is still that item 7 is absent
options.B: Yes; idempotency requires identical status codes and bodies
options.C: No; because DELETE is defined as a safe read-only method
options.D: Yes; DELETE must recreate the item before a retry

explanation: Idempotency concerns the intended effect on server state, not identical responses. Both requests leave the item absent, even if the second response differs.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: GET /accounts/7?close=true closes an account as its requested action. Which HTTP design issue is most direct?

options.A: It is correct solely because the URI uses a noun
options.B: It violates a rule that GET cannot contain a query string
options.C: It assigns a requested state-changing action to the safe GET method
options.D: It makes every response automatically uncacheable regardless of headers

explanation: GET is intended to be safe. Query parameters are allowed, but using one to request account closure violates safe-method semantics and risks unintended activation by automated retrieval.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A client has a cached GET representation tagged "v3". It sends If-None-Match: "v3", and the selected current representation still matches that validator. What response normally allows reuse of the cached representation?

options.A: 301 Moved Permanently with a new URI required
options.B: 201 Created with a second resource
options.C: 500 Internal Server Error because the validator matched
options.D: 304 Not Modified, without a response content body

explanation: For a conditional GET, a matching If-None-Match validator leads to 304. The client reuses its stored representation; the 304 does not carry a replacement representation body.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A server rejects an HTTP request because its request syntax is malformed. Which listed status is the direct client-error choice?

options.A: 404 Not Found
options.B: 503 Service Unavailable
options.C: 401 Unauthorized
options.D: 400 Bad Request

explanation: 400 covers malformed syntax and other perceived client-request errors. 401 concerns authentication, while 503 signals temporary service unavailability.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A protected endpoint receives no acceptable authentication credentials and challenges the client to authenticate. Which response pairing fits standard HTTP semantics?

options.A: 403 Forbidden with a mandatory Location redirect
options.B: 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate challenge
options.C: 200 OK with a mandatory WWW-Authenticate challenge
options.D: 502 Bad Gateway with a session identifier

explanation: 401 indicates the absence of valid authentication credentials for the target resource. The server must include at least one applicable WWW-Authenticate challenge.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A server authenticates a user successfully but refuses a requested operation because that user lacks the required role. It chooses to disclose this authorization refusal. Which status fits?

options.A: 301 Moved Permanently
options.B: 201 Created
options.C: 403 Forbidden
options.D: 401 Unauthorized solely because any refusal is an authentication failure

explanation: 403 expresses that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. The stated reason is authorization, not missing or invalid authentication.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: An origin server encounters an unexpected internal exception while processing an otherwise valid request and cannot complete it. Which general status fits this failure?

options.A: 400 Bad Request
options.B: 500 Internal Server Error
options.C: 201 Created
options.D: 304 Not Modified

explanation: 500 represents an unexpected server condition that prevents fulfillment. More specific gateway and temporary-unavailability conditions are not stated here.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Scenario A: a reverse proxy receives an invalid response from its upstream while serving a request. Scenario B: an origin server temporarily cannot serve requests because it is overloaded. Which status pairing is most precise?

options.A: A: 404 Not Found; B: 400 Bad Request
options.B: A: 503 Service Unavailable; B: 502 Bad Gateway
options.C: A: 200 OK; B: 301 Moved Permanently
options.D: A: 502 Bad Gateway; B: 503 Service Unavailable

explanation: 502 describes an invalid upstream response received by a gateway. 503 describes temporary inability to serve, such as overload or scheduled maintenance; Retry-After may describe a recovery delay.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Which design best satisfies REST constraints concerning stateless interactions, cacheability, and layered systems?

options.A: Each request carries needed interaction context, responses indicate caching rules, and clients need not know every intermediary layer
options.B: Every response must be unconditionally cached forever even when personalized
options.C: Every request depends on private conversational state stored only in the previous server process
options.D: Clients must bypass every intermediary and contact the origin implementation directly

explanation: REST combines self-contained interactions, explicit cache semantics, and a layered architecture. It does not require process-local conversational state, direct-only connections, or indiscriminate caching.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: In a conventional server-side login-session design, a browser stores an opaque session ID in a cookie. Where is the associated server-side session state normally stored?

options.A: Inside the Cookie header as an automatically embedded complete server memory snapshot
options.B: Necessarily inside localStorage because every cookie is a storage pointer
options.C: In a server-side session store indexed by that identifier
options.D: Necessarily inside the browser's sessionStorage because the word session is used

explanation: A server-side session ID identifies state held by the service, perhaps in a shared database or cache. A login session is not the same concept as the sessionStorage browser API.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Assume ordinary first-party pages with storage enabled and no additional partitioning distinctions. Which page shares the localStorage origin of https://example.com/app?

options.A: http://example.com/app
options.B: https://api.example.com/app
options.C: https://example.com:8443/app
options.D: https://example.com/other

explanation: Web Storage is associated with an origin, whose scheme, host, and effective port must match. A path change keeps the origin; the other choices change one of those components.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: Browser JavaScript on https://app.example wants to send a cross-origin PUT to https://api.example with Content-Type: application/json. No cached preflight permission exists. What permission-check request does CORS normally require first?

options.A: HEAD with Access-Control-Request-Method: GET
options.B: The PUT must always be sent directly without any preflight
options.C: POST with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set by the client
options.D: OPTIONS with Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT

explanation: PUT is not a CORS-safelisted method, and application/json is not a safelisted Content-Type. An OPTIONS preflight asks whether the target permits the actual method and relevant headers.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A browser fetch from https://app.example to https://api.example uses credentials: "include". Cookie policy permits the eligible cookie, the GET reaches the server, and no other blocking policy applies. The response headers are shown. Why can the script not read the response?
code_snippet:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Content-Type: application/json

{"balance": 42}

options.A: All cross-origin GET requests require a POST preflight first
options.B: Credentialed CORS requires a matching explicit allowed origin; wildcard * does not satisfy it
options.C: The request cannot have reached the server because every CORS error prevents network transmission
options.D: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials must be changed from true to false

explanation: With credentials mode include, Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be *. A matching explicit origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is needed to expose the response; read blocking does not prove the request was unsent.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A browser uses ordinary fetch to make a cross-origin POST with credentials: "omit", Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, no custom headers, and a simple string body. No other policy or transport restriction applies. The server accepts the request and changes its data but returns no CORS response headers. Which outcome is correct?

options.A: The POST can be sent and processed, but the browser blocks script access to its response
options.B: The response is always readable because the POST Content-Type is safelisted
options.C: Omitting CORS response headers automatically rolls back the server's data change
options.D: The browser must preflight every POST and never sends this one

explanation: This request does not require preflight under the stated conditions. Missing CORS permission prevents response exposure to the script; it does not undo a request the server has already processed.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: An API defines two PATCH documents with the exact sequential operations shown. Each resource starts with counter=3. Each document is applied twice to its own resource, without other writes. Considering only the intended counter state, which statement is correct?
code_snippet:
PATCH document A:
    set counter = 5
    increment counter by 1

PATCH document B:
    increment counter by 2

options.A: A is idempotent and ends at 6; B is not idempotent and ends at 7
options.B: Both are idempotent and both end at 6
options.C: A is non-idempotent and ends at 12; B is idempotent and ends at 5
options.D: Both are non-idempotent merely because the HTTP method is PATCH

explanation: A resets to 5 before incrementing, so each complete application ends at 6. B increments the existing state by two each time, producing 3->5->7. PATCH can be designed idempotently but is not generally guaranteed to be.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: A same-origin page stores token L in localStorage and has eligible login cookie S marked Secure and HttpOnly. An injected same-origin script executes with ordinary page privileges, and no additional policy blocks its requests. Which capability description is accurate?

options.A: It can read L and issue same-origin authenticated requests using S, but cannot directly read S through document.cookie
options.B: It can read S but localStorage is automatically hidden from same-origin JavaScript
options.C: It can read neither L nor S and cannot issue authenticated requests
options.D: It can read both L and S because HttpOnly affects only transport encryption

explanation: localStorage is script-accessible for the origin. HttpOnly hides S from script cookie-reading APIs, but the browser can still attach that eligible cookie to script-initiated requests. Secure restricts its transport to secure channels.

module: Module 4: Applied Systems, Cloud & Software Engineering
question: No preflight cache entry exists for the proposed cross-origin PUT. Its requested unsafe header names and the server's preflight response are shown. Credentials mode is omit, there are no redirects, and every other policy check passes. What does the browser do next?
code_snippet:
OPTIONS /items/7 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example
Origin: https://app.example
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: PUT
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type

options.A: Treat the OPTIONS 200 as the completed PUT response without sending the update
options.B: Send the PUT because allowing its method automatically allows every header
options.C: Fail the preflight and withhold the PUT because authorization is not allowed by Access-Control-Allow-Headers
options.D: Send the PUT but silently strip Authorization while retaining the application's intended request

explanation: The preflight must authorize the method and all relevant unsafe request headers. Content-Type alone does not authorize Authorization, so the actual PUT is not sent under these assumptions.
